arXiv:2510.20094v1 [math.PR] 23 Oct 2025

On the Structure of Stationary Solutions to McKean-Vlasov Equations with Applications to Noisy Transformers

Krishnakumar Balasubramanian1 Address: 1Department of Statistics, University of California, Davis, Email: kbala@ucdavis.edu , Sayan Banerjee2 Address: 2Department of Statistics and Operations Research, University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill. Email: sayan@email.unc.edu and Philippe Rigollet3 Address: 3Department of Mathematics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Email: rigollet@mit.edu
Abstract.

We study stationary solutions of McKean-Vlasov equations on the circle. Our main contributions stem from observing an exact equivalence between solutions of the stationary McKean-Vlasov equation and an infinite-dimensional quadratic system of equations over Fourier coefficients, which allows explicit characterization of the stationary states in a sequence space rather than a function space. This framework provides a transparent description of local bifurcations, characterizing their periodicity, and resonance structures, while accommodating singular potentials. We derive analytic expressions that characterize the emergence, form and shape (supercritical, critical, subcritical or transcritical) of bifurcations involving possibly multiple Fourier modes and connect them with discontinuous phase transitions. We also characterize, under suitable assumptions, the detailed structure of the stationary bifurcating solutions that are accurate upto an arbitrary number of Fourier modes. At the global level, we establish regularity and concavity properties of the free energy landscape, proving existence, compactness, and coexistence of globally minimizing stationary measures, further identifying discontinuous phase transitions with points of non-differentiability of the minimum free energy map. As an application, we specialize the theory to the Noisy Mean-Field Transformer model, where we show how changing the inverse temperature parameter β\beta affects the geometry of the infinitely many bifurcations from the uniform measure. We also explain how increasing β\beta can lead to a rich class of approximate multi-mode stationary solutions which can be seen as ‘metastable states’. Further, a sharp transition from continuous to discontinuous (first-order) phase behavior is observed as β\beta increases.

AMS 2020 subject classifications: 35Q83, 35Q70, 34K18, 60H50, 82C22, 35B27.

Keywords: McKean-Vlasov equations, stationary solutions, free energy, Noisy Transformers, bifurcation theory, phase transition, metastability, periodicity, Lyapunov-Schmidt reduction.

1. Introduction

Consider the following McKean-Vlasov equation on the circle 𝕊1=[0,2​π)\mathbb{S}^{1}=[0,2\pi):

(1.1) ∂tp=∂θ​θp−κ​∂θ(p​∂θ(W⋆p)),p∈C1,2​([0,∞)×𝕊1),\displaystyle\partial_{t}p=\partial_{\theta\theta}p-\kappa\partial_{\theta}(p\,\partial_{\theta}(W\star p)),\qquad p\in C^{1,2}([0,\infty)\times\mathbb{S}^{1}),

where W:[0,2​π)→ℝW:[0,2\pi)\to\mathbb{R} is the interaction potential,

(W⋆p)​(θ):=12​π​∫02​πW⁡(θ−ϕ)​p​(ϕ)​𝑑ϕ,(W\star p)(\theta):=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}W(\theta-\phi)\,p(\phi)\,\mathrm{d}\phi,

and we impose the normalization and positivity conditions

p⁡(⋅,⋅)≥0,12​π​∫02​πp⁡(⋅,θ)​𝑑θ=1,p(\cdot,\cdot)\geq 0,\qquad\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}p(\cdot,\theta)\,\mathrm{d}\theta=1,

so that p⁡(t,⋅)p(t,\cdot) defines a probability density on 𝕊1\mathbb{S}^{1} for each t≥0t\geq 0, and κ>0\kappa>0 represents the interaction intensity. Throughout this article, WW is assumed to be even, square integrable, and have the Fourier expansion W⁡(θ)=∑ℓ=1∞aℓ​cos⁡ℓ​θW(\theta)=\sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty}a_{\ell}\cos\ell\theta. Eq. 1.1 is a canonical nonlinear diffusion equation that arises as the mean-field limit, as N→∞N\to\infty, of systems of weakly interacting particles on 𝕊1\mathbb{S}^{1} whose angular dynamics evolve according to

(1.2) d​θi​(t)=κN​∑j=1N∂θW⁡(θi​(t)−θj​(t))​d​t+2​d​Bi​(t),1≤i≤N,d\theta_{i}(t)=\frac{\kappa}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\partial_{\theta}W(\theta_{i}(t)-\theta_{j}(t))\,dt+\sqrt{2}\,dB_{i}(t),\quad 1\leq i\leq N,

where B1,…,BNB_{1},\dots,B_{N} are independent standard Brownian motions. The term ∂θW⁡(θi−θj)\partial_{\theta}W(\theta_{i}-\theta_{j}) represents the interaction force exerted by particle jj on particle ii, governing the strength and direction of coupling: attractive potentials promote synchronization, while repulsive ones lead to dispersion or multimodal states. In the mean-field limit, these pairwise forces collectively produce the nonlinear drift term −κ∂θ(p∂θ(W⋆p))-\kappa\partial_{\theta}(p\,\partial_{\theta}(W\star p)) in Eq. 1.1, which combines with the diffusive term ∂θ​θp\partial_{\theta\theta}p to describe the evolution of the population density on 𝕊1\mathbb{S}^{1}. The McKean-Vlasov equation arises in a wide range of mean-field models, including synchronization dynamics (Kuramoto, 1981; Bertini et al., 2010), granular media (Bolley et al., 2013), collective behavior in biological systems (Keller and Segel, 1971), opinion dynamics (Hegselmann, 2015), to name a few.

Our primary interest lies in explicitly characterizing the stationary weak solutions to (1.1), which satisfy

(1.3) ∂θ​θp=κ​∂θ(p​∂θ(W⋆p)).\displaystyle\partial_{\theta\theta}p=\kappa\partial_{\theta}(p\,\partial_{\theta}(W\star p)).

Such stationary solutions approximate equilibria of the interacting particle system (1.2) and coincide with the critical points of the associated free energy functional ρ↦ℱ⁡(ρ,κ)\rho\mapsto\mathcal{F}(\rho,\kappa), where

ℱ⁡(ρ,κ):=12​π​∫02​πρ⁡(θ)​log⁡ρ⁡(θ)​𝑑θ−κ8​π2​∫02​π∫02​πW⁡(θ−ϕ)​ρ​(θ)​ρ​(ϕ)​𝑑θ​𝑑ϕ.\displaystyle\mathcal{F}(\rho,\kappa):=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\rho(\theta)\log\rho(\theta)\mathrm{d}\theta-\frac{\kappa}{8\pi^{2}}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}W(\theta-\phi)\rho(\theta)\rho(\phi)\mathrm{d}\theta\mathrm{d}\phi.

The uniform distribution on 𝕊1\mathbb{S}^{1} is a trivial stationary solution as both the left and right hand sides of (1.3) vanish with this choice of pp. Our primary focus is on the existence, shape and bifurcation structure of other, nontrivial, stationary solutions. A precise, explicit understanding of these equilibrium densities is crucial for several reasons. First, the structure and multiplicity of stationary solutions determine the possible long-time behaviors and phase transitions of the underlying mean-field dynamics. Second, the stability of these equilibria governs whether the system converges to the uniform distribution, organizes into coherent patterns, or exhibits abrupt discontinuous transitions as the interaction strength κ\kappa varies. Finally, obtaining detailed representations of pp in terms of WW and κ\kappa enables connecting qualitative features of the equilibrium density, such as periodicity and multi-modality, to the spectral properties of WW.

Analysis of stationary solutions to the McKean-Vlasov equation has traditionally been tackled in function spaces, often requiring advanced tools from calculus of variations; see, for example, Carrillo et al. (2020). A key feature that distinguishes the approach taken in this paper from previous ones is the observation that the problem of finding stationary solutions can be transformed exactly into finding solutions to an infinite-dimensional system of quadratic equations in a Fourier sequence space. This shift from a function space to a sequence space enables us to do a more transparent and elaborate analysis.

1.1. Background and challenges

Long-time behavior for McKean-Vlasov equations is a subject of extensive current research. Most of the existing results in this direction assume some form of convexity. This is either incorporated via the uniform convexity of WW—for McKean-Vlasov equations on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}—or by introducing a uniformly convex confinement potential VV as an additional term −∂θ(p∂θV)-\partial_{\theta}(p\partial_{\theta}V) in the RHS of (1.1) which overcomes the lack of convexity of WW; see, for example, Carrillo et al. (2003); Malrieu (2003); Cattiaux et al. (2008); Guillin and Monmarché (2021). In this case, the free energy functional inherits convexity properties and, in particular, admits a unique global minimizer, sometimes up to translations. This greatly simplifies the energy landscape and, in addition, one also obtains rates of convergence to stationarity by viewing (1.1) as a gradient flow for the free energy on the L2L^{2}-Wasserstein space and applying log-Sobolev inequalities. In our setting, there is no confinement potential and the inherent periodicity of WW, due to the underlying manifold 𝕊1\mathbb{S}^{1}, forbids it from being convex. This results in a very rich free energy landscape and makes the analysis challenging.

For the non-convex case, early works on stationary solutions and phase transitions for McKean–Vlasov (and related Vlasov–Fokker–Planck) equations focus on existence questions and qualitative behavior for specialized interaction functions. Dawson (1983) establishes critical dynamics and fluctuation results for mean-field cooperative models with double-well confinement and Curie–Weiss-type interaction potentials. Yozo (1984) analyzes bifurcations, showing non-uniqueness of stationary solutions for the McKean–Vlasov equation on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. For the double-well confinement potential case, Tugaut (2014) provides a quantitative description of bifurcations and the multiplicity of invariant measures, clarifying how the double-well structure drives phase transitions.

Work on phase transitions and bifurcation structures for spatially periodic or finite-volume problems advances rapidly in recent years. Chayes and Panferov (2010) analyze the free energy functional for general interaction potentials on 𝕋d\mathbb{T}^{d} and characterize the continuity of phase transitions for its global minimizers as κ\kappa varies. In particular, they show that when all Fourier coefficients of WW are negative, the free energy becomes convex in a suitable sense and the uniform distribution on 𝕋d\mathbb{T}^{d} is the unique minimizer of ℱ⁡(κ,⋅)\mathcal{F}(\kappa,\cdot) for all κ\kappa. This implies that non-trivial stationary distributions arise only when WW admits at least one positive Fourier mode. Closest in theme to our work is Carrillo et al. (2020), who provide criteria for local bifurcations from the uniform distribution based on positive Fourier modes of WW and give sufficient conditions for both continuous and discontinuous phase transitions on the torus. Their analysis requires intricate calculus on function spaces: the bifurcation study involves fixed points of a map on L2​(𝕋d)L^{2}(\mathbb{T}^{d}), where the associated Fréchet derivatives make the approach difficult to extend beyond single-mode bifurcations (see Remark 2.1). This framework is recently extended to the sphere 𝕊d\mathbb{S}^{d} by Shalova and Schlichting (2024).

1.2. Our contributions

1.2.1. General results on stationary McKean-Vlasov equations on 𝕊1\mathbb{S}^{1}

In this work, we develop a Fourier-analytic framework for analyzing (1.3), which transforms the nonlinear PDE into an infinite-dimensional system of quadratic equations in a Fourier space; see Theorem 2.1. This representation provides a transparent description of stationary solutions as the zeroes of the map F:ℓw2×ℝ+→ℓ2F:\ell^{2}_{w}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}\rightarrow\ell^{2} given by

Fℓ​(p¯,κ)=ℓ⁡(2−κ​aℓ)​pℓ−κ​∑j<ℓj​aj​pj​pℓ−j−κ​∑j>ℓ(j​aj−(j−ℓ)​aj−ℓ)​pj​pj−ℓ,ℓ≥1,\displaystyle F_{\ell}(\underline{p},\kappa)=\ell(2-\kappa a_{\ell})p_{\ell}-\kappa\sum_{j<\ell}ja_{j}p_{j}p_{\ell-j}-\kappa\sum_{j>\ell}(ja_{j}-(j-\ell)a_{j-\ell})p_{j}p_{j-\ell},\ \ell\geq 1,

where ℓw2:={p¯∈ℝ∞:∑ℓ=1∞(1+ℓ2)​pℓ2<∞}\ell^{2}_{w}:=\{\underline{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{\infty}:\sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty}(1+\ell^{2})p_{\ell}^{2}<\infty\} and ℓ2:={p¯∈ℝ∞:∑ℓ=1∞pℓ2<∞}\ell^{2}:=\{\underline{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{\infty}:\sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty}p_{\ell}^{2}<\infty\}. Technically, this transfers the analysis from function spaces treated in Carrillo et al. (2020) to more tractable sequence spaces, thereby enabling the investigation of more detailed properties of stationary solutions. As a first step, we adapt the Crandall-Rabinowitz (Crandall and Rabinowitz, 1971) setup used in Carrillo et al. (2020) to our function FF in Theorem 2.2 that gives rise to non-trivial bifurcating solutions at intensity values κ=2/aℓ∗\kappa=2/a_{\ell^{*}}, where aℓ∗a_{\ell^{*}} is a positive Fourier mode of WW such that aj≠aℓ∗a_{j}\neq a_{\ell^{*}} for j≠ℓ∗j\neq\ell^{*}. In comparison to Carrillo et al. (2020, Theorem 4.2), our result applies to more singular potentials WW and also clarifies how the bifurcating branches ‘bend’ forward or backward (supercritical or subcritical bifurcations; see Fig. 1) based on the sign of the ratio

(1.4) Rℓ∗​(W)≔aℓ∗−2​a2​ℓ∗aℓ∗−a2​ℓ∗,\displaystyle R_{\ell^{*}}(W)\coloneqq\frac{a_{\ell^{*}}-2a_{2\ell^{*}}}{a_{\ell^{*}}-a_{2\ell^{*}}},

which we refer to as the ℓ∗\ell^{*}-signature of WW. In Theorem 2.3, we characterize the periodicity of non-trivial bifurcating solutions and, in particular, show that if a bifurcation point arises from possibly multiple coinciding Fourier modes of WW, then any non-trivial bifurcating solution has to be gg-periodic, where gg is the greatest common divisor of the indices of the coinciding Fourier modes. As a consequence, if a1>a2>⋯>0a_{1}>a_{2}>\dots>0, the periodicity of bifurcating branches at the subsequent bifurcation points 2/a1<2/a2<…2/a_{1}<2/a_{2}<\dots increases.

In the setting of Carrillo et al. (2020, Theorem 4.2) and our Theorem 2.2, the uniqueness assertion aj≠aℓ∗a_{j}\neq a_{\ell^{*}} for j≠ℓ∗j\neq\ell^{*} leads to single mode bifurcating branches around κ=2/aℓ∗\kappa=2/a_{\ell^{*}} where, locally, only one Fourier mode of the solution dominates. In Theorem 2.4, we characterize multi-mode branches when multiple Fourier coefficients of WW cluster around the same value. This leads to a rich class of bifurcations. As a special case, under the ‘resonance assumption’ aℓ=am=aℓ+ma_{\ell}=a_{m}=a_{\ell+m}, we obtain transcritical bifurcations under suitable assumptions (see Fig. 1). This analysis helps us construct a broad family of ‘approximately’ stationary (metastable) solutions of (1.1) when multiple Fourier modes of WW are close to each other (see Remark 2.5). In Theorem 2.5, under slightly stronger assumptions on WW than in Theorem 2.2, we give a very detailed structural characterization of the stationary solutions that are locally accurate up to an arbitrary level of precision at the exponential scale.

In Section 2.6, we study phase transitions which correspond to a shift in the energy minimizing branch from the uniform distribution to a non-uniform one as κ\kappa increases, see Definition 2.2. We connect the shape of bifurcations to the continuity of phase transitions and show that bifurcations that have a branch in the decreasing κ\kappa direction (e.g. subcritical and transcritical bifurcations) lead to discontinuous phase transitions of the free energy minimizers; see Theorem 2.6 and Fig. 4. Corollary 2.1 exhibits instances when this happens and, in particular, shows that the sufficient condition for discontinuous phase transition in Carrillo et al. (2020, Theorem 5.11) is just one of many instances of creating such a bifurcation that ‘turns back’. This analysis also paints a geometric picture for such transitions visualized in Fig. 4: the observed discontinuity in the dynamics arising in the increasing κ\kappa direction emerges, in fact, in a continuous fashion through a bifurcation in the decreasing κ\kappa direction.

In Section 3, we present some global properties of the energy landscape. As explicitly computable special cases for the zeros of the map FF above, we present a global bifurcation picture involving Poisson kernels for the singular potential W⁡(θ)=−log⁡(2​sin⁡(θ/2))W(\theta)=-\log(2\sin(\theta/2)) (Theorem 3.1) and a global ‘Kuramoto type’ branch when WW has a finite number of non-zero Fourier modes, all positive (Theorem 3.2). Finally, in Theorem 3.3, we perform a detailed analysis of the free energy minimizing branch of solutions and, among other things, show that discontinuous phase transitions are connected to points of non-differentiability of the minimum free energy map κ↦m⁡(κ):=minρ⁡ℱ⁡(κ,ρ)\kappa\mapsto m(\kappa):=\min_{\rho}\mathcal{F}(\kappa,\rho).

We remark here that, to cleanly demonstrate our main results, our main focus in this work is for the case of McKean-Vlasov equations on the circle. Nevertheless, our approach can be generalized to higher-dimensional compact manifolds like the dd-dimensional torus 𝕋d\mathbb{T}^{d} and sphere 𝕊d\mathbb{S}^{d}, which admit ‘Fourier expansions’ in terms of the associated orthonormal basis of L2L^{2} functions.

1.2.2. Applications to noisy mean-field transformers

Having established the general Fourier-analytic theory, we next demonstrate its utility by applying it to the noisy mean-field transformer model, an important modern instance of McKean–Vlasov dynamics. Recent works have focused on describing signal propagation in attention-based transformer architectures in the zero-noise setup (Geshkovski et al., 2024; Geshkovski et al., 2025; Bruno et al., 2025a; Chen et al., 2025; Burger et al., 2025; Castin et al., 2025; Bruno et al., 2025b). Our focus in this work is on the noisy setup, also considered recently in Shalova and Schlichting (2024). Studying the noisy regime provides a principled first step to understand how randomness in the intermediate multi-layer perceptron layers of transformer models affects stability, phase transitions, and emergent collective behavior in the overall large-scale transformer dynamics. In particular, it provides insight into how feature representations stabilize across layers in large-depth transformer models.

The Noisy mean-field Transformer potential is given by

(1.5) Wβ​(θ)≔eβ​cos⁡θ−1β=∑ℓ=1∞aℓ​(β)​cos⁡(ℓ​θ),β>0,\displaystyle W_{\beta}(\theta)\coloneqq\frac{e^{\beta\cos\theta}-1}{\beta}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty}a_{\ell}(\beta)\cos(\ell\theta),\qquad\beta>0,

where we have the explicit Fourier coefficients

aℓ(β)=2​Iℓ​(β)β,ℓ≥1,withIℓ(β)≔12​π∫02​πeβ​cos⁡ϕcos(ℓϕ)dϕ\displaystyle a_{\ell}(\beta)=\frac{2I_{\ell}(\beta)}{\beta},\quad\ell\geq 1,\quad\text{with}\quad I_{\ell}(\beta)\coloneqq\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}e^{\beta\cos\phi}\cos(\ell\phi)\,\mathrm{d}\phi

denoting the modified Bessel function of the first kind.

By applying our general Fourier-analytic framework to this model, we uncover a rich phase structure dependent on the noise parameter β\beta. In Section 2.2 we show that the uniform solution in the noisy mean-field Transformer model loses stability when κ>β/I1​(β)\kappa>\beta/I_{1}(\beta), marking the first bifurcation point. More generally, there are infinitely many bifurcations at κℓ∗​(β)=β/Iℓ​(β)\kappa_{\ell}^{*}(\beta)=\beta/I_{\ell}(\beta), each corresponding to the ℓ\ell-th Fourier mode, whose type (supercritical or subcritical) is governed by the ℓ\ell-signature of Wβ​(θ)W_{\beta}(\theta), i.e., the sign of Rℓ​(Wβ​(θ))≔Rℓ​(β)=(Iℓ​(β)−2​I2​ℓ​(β))/(Iℓ​(β)−I2​ℓ​(β))R_{\ell}(W_{\beta}(\theta))\coloneqq R_{\ell}(\beta)=(I_{\ell}(\beta)-2I_{2\ell}(\beta))/(I_{\ell}(\beta)-I_{2\ell}(\beta)). For small β\beta, all bifurcations are supercritical (bend right). As β\beta increases, the first few bifurcations become subcritical, and in the large-β\beta limit, every bifurcation approaches criticality from the subcritical side.

Another consequence of our general results, as shown in Section 2.4.1, is that in the large-β\beta regime, the Fourier coefficients of the Noisy Transformer potential, aℓ​(β)=2​Iℓ​(β)/βa_{\ell}(\beta)=2I_{\ell}(\beta)/\beta, become increasingly clustered: for fixed LL, the relative difference between al1​(β)a_{l_{1}}(\beta) and al2​(β)a_{l_{2}}(\beta) scales as (ℓ22−ℓ12)/(2​β)(\ell_{2}^{2}-\ell_{1}^{2})/(2\beta). Consequently, for β≳L2/(2​ε)\beta\gtrsim L^{2}/(2\varepsilon), the first LL modes are nearly degenerate, and the bifurcation thresholds κℓ∗​(β)=β/Iℓ​(β)\kappa_{\ell}^{*}(\beta)=\beta/I_{\ell}(\beta) accumulate exponentially fast as β→∞\beta\to\infty. This near-degeneracy activates higher-order bifurcation interactions, giving rise to a family of metastable stationary states analogous to those observed in the noiseless Transformer (Geshkovski et al., 2024; Bruno et al., 2025a). In Section 2.5.1, we use the refined approximation described in Theorem 2.5 to dive deeper into the structure of the bifurcating solutions. We exhibit how the primary mode of the stationary density interacts with the other modes and offer an interactive way to visualize the different possible shapes that emerge as β,κ\beta,\kappa vary (see Fig. 3).

Finally, in Theorem 2.7, we show that the phase transition behavior, in the sense of Definition 2.2, of the Noisy Transformer is governed by the quantity R⁡(β)=I2​(β)/I1​(β)R(\beta)=I_{2}(\beta)/I_{1}(\beta), which increases monotonically with β\beta. There exist thresholds 0<β−<β+0<\beta_{-}<\beta_{+} such that for β≤β−\beta\leq\beta_{-}, the transition at κ∗​(β)=β/I1​(β)\kappa^{*}(\beta)=\beta/I_{1}(\beta) is continuous (supercritical), while for β>β+\beta>\beta_{+}, it becomes discontinuous (subcritical) with a new critical point κc​(β)<κ∗​(β)\kappa_{c}(\beta)<\kappa^{*}(\beta). The crossover occurs near β+≈R−1​(1/2)≃2.447\beta_{+}\approx R^{-1}(1/2)\simeq 2.447, marking the shift from supercritical to subcritical bifurcation behavior.

Utility of adding ‘small noise’ to Transformer dynamics: Self-attention based transformer dynamics are noiseless. The above discussion indicates the possible utility of adding noise, potentially via the multilayer perceptrons interspersed with attention in actual Transformer models, and tuning its strength by varying κ\kappa (here, large κ\kappa is equivalent to ‘small noise’). As noted in Geshkovski et al. (2025), all points eventually collapse on running the noiseless Transformer dynamics long enough. Without noise, the undulations in WW arising from different Fourier modes translates into a highly uneven landscape for the free energy functional, now without the entropy term, which gives rise to metastable states at several scales. As a result, although there is eventual collapse, there could be intermediate clustering in intricate ways, depending on the initial density profile of the points, and a full understanding of this phenomenon is quite involved; see Geshkovski et al. (2024); Karagodin et al. (2024); Bruno et al. (2025a) for some results in this direction. Adding and tuning the noise helps regularize the energy profile at ‘small enough’ scales while retaining its features at ‘large enough’ scales. This gives control on the expressivity of the Transformer. Moreover, the noise prevents eventual collapse and stationary states are ‘truly stationary’.

1.3. Additional related works

Among other related works, recently Bertoli et al. (2024) study related notions of stability when WW has a finite number of non-zero Fourier modes and present heuristic, numerical analyses for the existence of multimodal stationary states.  Cormier (2022) provides conditions guaranteeing local exponential stability of invariant measures using Lions-derivative techniques and analytic-function/Fourier-based criteria in different settings, giving explicit, checkable tests that are immediately useful in applications such as neuronal mean-field models. Vukadinovic (2023) analyzes bifurcation thresholds for a two-component weakly-coupled Hodgkin–Huxley neurons and produces a finite-dimensional reduction that makes the bifurcation explicit in that application.  Zhang (2025) gives a rigorous local bifurcation criterion for a large class of gradient-type McKean-Vlasov problems using regularized determinants and operator-theoretic tools; this provides a direct route to relate linearization spectra on function spaces to phase transition thresholds.

Furthermore, Degond et al. (2015) study phase transitions and long-time behavior in kinetic models of self-propelled particles and alignment-type interactions; their analyses emphasize kinetic, as opposed to purely gradient, structure and connect phase transitions to changes in macroscopic order parameters and, in certain settings, hysteresis. These kinetic perspectives are relevant when one moves beyond overdamped gradient flows to retain inertial or alignment dynamics.

While finalizing this work, we became aware of the concurrent study by Gerber et al. (2025), which investigates the dynamical behavior and coarsening phenomena in weakly interacting diffusions in a rich family of models that includes noisy transformers. Their results are complementary to ours: whereas we investigate the structure and bifurcation of stationary solutions at the mean-field PDE level, their focus is primarily on the evolution and metastability of clustered states at the particle dynamics level.

1.4. Solution spaces

In this work, it will be convenient to consider weak solutions for (1.3) in more general spaces. We denote by Ls2​(𝕊1)L_{s}^{2}(\mathbb{S}^{1}) the space of square integrable functions ff on 𝕊1\mathbb{S}^{1} such that f⁡(θ−π)=f⁡(π−θ),∀θ∈[0,2​π)f(\theta-\pi)=f(\pi-\theta),\forall\theta\in[0,2\pi) (even function). We consider solutions in the Sobolev space

Hs1(𝕊1):=𝒲s1,2(𝕊1)={p:𝕊1→ℝ|p,p′∈Ls2(𝕊1)}.H_{s}^{1}(\mathbb{S}^{1}):=\mathcal{W}_{s}^{1,2}(\mathbb{S}^{1})=\Bigl\{\,p:\mathbb{S}^{1}\to\mathbb{R}\,\Big|\,p,\,p^{\prime}\in L_{s}^{2}(\mathbb{S}^{1})\Bigr\}.

consisting of square-integrable, even functions on the circle whose weak derivative is also square-integrable, equipped with the usual Sobolev norm ‖p‖H12:=∫02​π(p2​(θ)+|p′​(θ)|2)​𝑑θ\|p\|_{H^{1}}^{2}:=\smallint_{0}^{2\pi}\big(p^{2}(\theta)+|p^{\prime}(\theta)|^{2}\big)\,d\theta. The symmetry assumption is both natural and nonrestrictive: it corresponds to considering equilibria invariant under reflection, a property inherited from our assumption that WW is even.

2. Local properties

2.1. A Fourier representation

The starting point of our analysis is the following equivalent representation of a solution pp to (1.3) purely in terms of Fourier modes of pp and WW. This enables us to perform a more tractable and detailed analysis of stationary solutions on sequence spaces in comparison to analysis on function spaces in Carrillo et al. (2020). The generality of the following proposition also helps us analyze more singular potentials WW.

Theorem 2.1.

Fix κ>0\kappa>0. Let pp be any solution to (1.3) in Hs1​(𝕊1)H_{s}^{1}(\mathbb{S}^{1}). Write

p⁡(θ)=2​∑ℓ=0∞pℓ​cos⁡ℓ​θ,θ∈[0,2​π).\displaystyle p(\theta)=2\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}p_{\ell}\cos\ell\theta,\quad\theta\in[0,2\pi).

Then, {pℓ:ℓ≥0}\{p_{\ell}:\ell\geq 0\} satisfy p0=1/2p_{0}=1/2 and for ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1,

(2.1) ℓ⁡(2−κ​aℓ)​pℓ=κ​∑j<ℓj​aj​pj​pℓ−j+κ​∑j>ℓ(j​aj−(j−ℓ)​aj−ℓ)​pj​pj−ℓ.\displaystyle\ell(2-\kappa a_{\ell})p_{\ell}=\kappa\sum_{j<\ell}ja_{j}p_{j}p_{\ell-j}+\kappa\sum_{j>\ell}(ja_{j}-(j-\ell)a_{j-\ell})p_{j}p_{j-\ell}.

Conversely, any p∈Hs1​(𝕊1)p\in H_{s}^{1}(\mathbb{S}^{1}) whose Fourier coefficients satisfy the above is a solution to (1.3). Moreover, any such solution satisfies the fixed point equation

where Z=∫02​πexp⁡(κ​∑ℓ=1∞pℓ​aℓ​cos⁡ℓ​ψ)​𝑑ψZ=\int_{0}^{2\pi}\exp\left(\kappa\sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty}p_{\ell}a_{\ell}\cos\ell\psi\right)\mathrm{d}\psi.

Since pp will always satisfy 12​π​∫02​πp⁡(⋅,θ)​𝑑θ=1\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}p(\cdot,\theta)\mathrm{d}\theta=1, we suppress the zeroth mode and simply call p¯=(pℓ:=12​π​∫02​πp⁡(⋅,θ)​cos⁡ℓ​θ​𝑑θ)ℓ∈ℕ\underline{p}=\left(p_{\ell}:=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}p(\cdot,\theta)\cos\ell\theta\mathrm{d}\theta\right)_{\ell\in\mathbb{N}} the Fourier modes of pp. Observe that the Fourier modes of p∈Hs1​(𝕊1)p\in H_{s}^{1}(\mathbb{S}^{1}) correspond exactly with the weighted ℓ2\ell^{2} space

ℓw2:={x¯∈ℝ∞:∑ℓ=1∞(1+ℓ2)​xℓ2<∞}.\ell^{2}_{w}:=\{\underline{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{\infty}:\sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty}(1+\ell^{2})x_{\ell}^{2}<\infty\}.

(2.2) F⁡(p¯,κ)=0¯,F(\underline{p},\kappa)=\underline{0},

where F:ℓw2×ℝ+→ℓ2F:\ell^{2}_{w}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}\rightarrow\ell^{2} given by

We now define the notions of bifurcation point and bifurcation curve.

Definition 2.1.

A point (p¯b,κb)(\underline{p}_{b},\kappa_{b}) is called a bifurcation point of the map FF if (p¯b,κb)(\underline{p}_{b},\kappa_{b}) lies in the closure of the set {(p¯,κ)∈ℓw2×ℝ+:F(p¯,κ)=0¯,p¯≠p¯b,κ≠κb}\{(\underline{p},\kappa)\in\ell^{2}_{w}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}:F(\underline{p},\kappa)=\underline{0},\ \underline{p}\neq\underline{p}_{b},\ \kappa\neq\kappa_{b}\}.

Further, if there exists δ>0\delta>0 and a continuous curve s↦(p¯​(s),κ​(s))s\mapsto(\underline{p}(s),\kappa(s)) mapping (−δ,δ)(-\delta,\delta) to ℓw2×ℝ+\ell^{2}_{w}\times\mathbb{R}_{+} such that F​(p¯​(s),κ​(s))=0F(\underline{p}(s),\kappa(s))=0 for all s∈(−δ,δ)s\in(-\delta,\delta), then this curve is called a bifurcation curve. If the bifurcation curve meets the bifurcation point at at most one ss, we call it a non-trivial branch of solutions.

Clearly, p¯≡0¯\underline{p}\equiv\underline{0} is a solution for all κ\kappa. This corresponds to p0≔Unif​(𝕊1)p_{0}\coloneqq\text{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{1}), which is always a stationary solution. We call κ↦(0¯,κ)\kappa\mapsto(\underline{0},\kappa) the ‘trivial’ branch of stationary solutions.

2.2. First order bifurcations

The next result characterizes the bifurcation points of FF about this trivial branch that are of first order, namely, they are related to a unique Fourier mode of WW.

Theorem 2.2.

Suppose supℓ≥1ℓ​|aℓ|<∞\sup_{\ell\geq 1}\ell|a_{\ell}|<\infty. Assume, for some ℓ∗∈ℕ\ell^{*}\in\mathbb{N}, aℓ∗>0a_{\ell^{*}}>0 and aℓ≠aℓ∗a_{\ell}\neq a_{\ell^{*}} for all ℓ≠ℓ∗\ell\neq\ell^{*}. Then, κ∗:=2/aℓ∗\kappa^{*}:=2/a_{\ell^{*}} is a pitchfork bifurcation point of FF in the sense that there exists δ>0\delta>0 and a non-trivial branch of solutions (p¯​(s),κ⁡(s)):(−δ,δ)→ℓw2×ℝ+(\underline{p}(s),\kappa(s)):(-\delta,\delta)\rightarrow\ell^{2}_{w}\times\mathbb{R}_{+} such that

p¯​(s)=s​eℓ∗+o⁡(s),\displaystyle\underline{p}(s)=se_{\ell^{*}}+o(s),

where {ej}j\{e_{j}\}_{j} is the canonical basis of ℓ2\ell^{2} and κ⁡(⋅)\kappa(\cdot) is twice differentiable and satisfies κ⁡(0)=κ∗,κ′​(0)=0\kappa(0)=\kappa^{*},\kappa^{\prime}(0)=0 and

(2.3) κ′′​(0)=2aℓ∗⋅Rℓ∗​(W)=2aℓ∗⋅aℓ∗−2​a2​ℓ∗aℓ∗−a2​ℓ∗.\displaystyle\kappa^{\prime\prime}(0)=\frac{2}{a_{\ell^{*}}}\cdot R_{\ell^{*}}(W)=\frac{2}{a_{\ell^{*}}}\cdot\frac{a_{\ell^{*}}-2a_{2\ell^{*}}}{a_{\ell^{*}}-a_{2\ell^{*}}}.

Moreover, (p¯​(s),κ​(s))(\underline{p}(s),\kappa(s)) comprise the only even non-trivial solution to (2.2) in a neighborhood of (0¯,κ∗)(\underline{0},\kappa^{*}) in ℓw2×ℝ+\ell^{2}_{w}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}. Further, if κ∉{2/aℓ:ℓ∈ℕ}\kappa\notin\{2/a_{\ell}\,:\,\ell\in\mathbb{N}\}, then κ\kappa cannot be a bifurcation point.

Remark 2.1.

Theorem 2.2 closely resembles Carrillo et al. (2020, Theorem 4.2 and Corollary 4.3). However, there are several key differences, as highlighted below.

  • (i)

    Carrillo et al. (2020, Theorem 4.2 and Corollary 4.3) study bifurcation points and associated solutions for the equation Fcgps​(ρ,κ)=0F_{\textsc{cgps}}(\rho,\kappa)=0, where Fcgps:Ls2​(𝕊1)×ℝ+→Ls2​(𝕊1)F_{\textsc{cgps}}:L_{s}^{2}(\mathbb{S}^{1})\times\mathbb{R}_{+}\rightarrow L_{s}^{2}(\mathbb{S}^{1}) corresponds to a fixed point equation for the associated McKean-Vlasov equation given by

    (2.4) Fcgps​(ρ,κ):=ρ−1Z​eκ​W⋆ρ,\displaystyle F_{\textsc{cgps}}(\rho,\kappa):=\rho-\frac{1}{Z}e^{\kappa W\star\rho},

    where Z:=12​π​∫02​πeκ​(W⋆ρ)​(s)​𝑑sZ:=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}e^{\kappa(W\star\rho)(s)}\mathrm{d}s is the normalizing factor. Although their result exhibits bifurcations for FcgpsF_{\textsc{cgps}} when W∈Ls2​(𝕊1)W\in L_{s}^{2}(\mathbb{S}^{1}), it can be directly related to bifurcations for solutions of the stationary McKean-Vlasov equation (1.3) only when WW has higher regularity, namely, W∈Hs1​(𝕊1)W\in H_{s}^{1}(\mathbb{S}^{1}) (see Carrillo et al. (2020, Theorem 2.3 and Proposition 2.4)). For the Keller-Segel model treated in Carrillo et al. (2020, Section 6.5), which has a potential not in Hs1​(𝕊1)H_{s}^{1}(\mathbb{S}^{1}), a case-specific argument is required. In comparison, the bifurcation theory for FF, treated in Theorem 2.2, is in one-to-one correspondence with that for solutions of (1.3) for any WW satisfying supℓ≥0ℓ​|aℓ|<∞\sup_{\ell\geq 0}\ell|a_{\ell}|<\infty, which allows for more singular WW in Ls2​(𝕊1)L_{s}^{2}(\mathbb{S}^{1}). Moreover, the conclusion that there are no bifurcation points other than the ones of the form 2/aℓ,ℓ∈ℕ2/a_{\ell},\,\ell\in\mathbb{N}, carries over to solutions of (1.3) via this equivalence to zeros of FF.

  • (ii)

    FcgpsF_{\textsc{cgps}} is defined on a function space and involves exponential mappings, which makes the associated calculus quite intricate and prone to errors. In comparison, FF is a quadratic function on a sequence space which makes it significantly easier to analyze. In Carrillo et al. (2020, Theorem 4.2), working with Fréchet derivatives of FcgpsF_{\textsc{cgps}} led to an error in computing κ′′​(0)\kappa^{\prime\prime}(0), the curvature of the bifurcation curve (Kielhöfer (2012, Equation (I.6.11)) was erroneously applied), which gave a curvature κ′′​(0)=4​π​κ∗/3\kappa^{\prime\prime}(0)=4\pi\kappa^{*}/3 that is always positive irrespective of the choice of WW. Eq. 2.3 gives the correct curvature. We see that the bifurcation can be subcritical (left-sided), critical (vertical in the sense κ′′​(0)=0\kappa^{\prime\prime}(0)=0) or supercritical (right-sided) depending on the behavior of the quantity aℓ∗−2​a2​ℓ∗aℓ∗−a2​ℓ∗\frac{a_{\ell^{*}}-2a_{2\ell^{*}}}{a_{\ell^{*}}-a_{2\ell^{*}}}. This will also be useful later in quantifying discontinuous phase transitions (see Section 2.6).

2.2.1. Specialization to noisy mean-field transformers

We now specialize to the noisy mean-field transformer. Recall that this model employs the potential WβW_{\beta} defined in (1.5). From results in Gates and Penrose (1970) (see also (Chayes and Panferov, 2010, Proposition 2.9)), it follows that the uniform solution loses stability when κ>2/a1=β/I1​(β)\kappa>2/a_{1}=\beta/I_{1}(\beta). This also corresponds to the first bifurcation point. It can be checked that the map ℓ↦Iℓ​(β)\ell\mapsto I_{\ell}(\beta) is strictly decreasing for any β>0\beta>0. Thus, substituting the corresponding coefficients into Theorem 2.2 yields that, for any ℓ∈ℕ\ell\in\mathbb{N}, there is a bifurcation point at

κℓ∗​(β)=2aℓ​(β)=βIℓ​(β),\kappa_{\ell}^{*}(\beta)=\frac{2}{a_{\ell}(\beta)}=\frac{\beta}{I_{\ell}(\beta)},

corresponding to the ℓ\ell-th Fourier mode of WβW_{\beta}. This fact is likewise observed for Noisy Transformers on the sphere in Shalova and Schlichting (2024, Proposition 6.1).

By Theorem 2.2, the curvature of the bifurcating branch at the ℓ\ell-th bifurcation point is given explicitly by

κ′′​(0)=β⁡(Iℓ​(β)−2​I2​ℓ​(β))Iℓ​(β)​(Iℓ​(β)−I2​ℓ​(β)).\kappa^{\prime\prime}(0)=\frac{\beta\bigl(I_{\ell}(\beta)-2I_{2\ell}(\beta)\bigr)}{I_{\ell}(\beta)\bigl(I_{\ell}(\beta)-I_{2\ell}(\beta)\bigr)}.

Rℓ​(β)=aℓ−2​a2​ℓaℓ−a2​ℓ=Iℓ​(β)−2​I2​ℓ​(β)Iℓ​(β)−I2​ℓ​(β).R_{\ell}(\beta)\;=\;\frac{a_{\ell}-2a_{2\ell}}{a_{\ell}-a_{2\ell}}\;=\;\frac{I_{\ell}(\beta)-2I_{2\ell}(\beta)}{I_{\ell}(\beta)-I_{2\ell}(\beta)}.

Note that Rℓ​(β)R_{\ell}(\beta) is a strictly decreasing function of I2​ℓ​(β)Iℓ​(β)\frac{I_{2\ell}(\beta)}{I_{\ell}(\beta)}. From Turán-type inequalities (see Baricz (2010)),

Ik2​(β)≥Ik−1​(β)​Ik+1​(β)I_{k}^{2}(\beta)\geq I_{k-1}(\beta)I_{k+1}(\beta)

for all k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} and β>0\beta>0. This implies that the map k↦Ik+1​(β)Ik​(β)k\mapsto\frac{I_{k+1}(\beta)}{I_{k}(\beta)} is decreasing in kk. Hence,

is decreasing in ℓ\ell. Combining these observations, we conclude that ℓ↦Rℓ​(β)\ell\mapsto R_{\ell}(\beta) is increasing in ℓ\ell for every β>0\beta>0. Moreover, as β↦I2​ℓ​(β)Iℓ​(β)\beta\mapsto\frac{I_{2\ell}(\beta)}{I_{\ell}(\beta)} is strictly increasing in β\beta, which can again be verified using Turán-type inequalities, we have β↦Rℓ​(β)\beta\mapsto R_{\ell}(\beta) is strictly decreasing in β\beta for fixed ℓ∈ℕ\ell\in\mathbb{N}. 2.3. Periodicity

The next result gives periodicity properties of non-trivial solutions.

Theorem 2.3.

Suppose supℓ≥1ℓ​|aℓ|<∞\sup_{\ell\geq 1}\ell|a_{\ell}|<\infty.

(a) Assume, for some m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N}, am>0a_{m}>0 and aℓ​m≠ama_{\ell m}\neq a_{m} for all ℓ>1\ell>1. Then, there exists a non-trivial mm-periodic branch of solutions (p¯​(s),κ⁡(s)):(−δ,δ)→ℓw2×ℝ+(\underline{p}(s),\kappa(s)):(-\delta,\delta)\rightarrow\ell^{2}_{w}\times\mathbb{R}_{+} at bifurcation point 2/am2/a_{m} that has the following description. Let W(m)​(θ):=∑ℓ=1∞aℓ​m​cos⁡ℓ​θ,θ∈[0,2​π),W^{(m)}(\theta):=\sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty}a_{\ell m}\cos\ell\theta,\ \theta\in[0,2\pi), and consider the unique non-trivial branch of solutions (p¯(m)​(s),κ(m)​(s)):(−δ(m),δ(m))→ℓw2×ℝ+(\underline{p}^{(m)}(s),\kappa^{(m)}(s)):(-\delta^{(m)},\delta^{(m)})\rightarrow\ell^{2}_{w}\times\mathbb{R}_{+} at bifurcation point κm:=2/am\kappa_{m}:=2/a_{m} for (1.3) with potential W(m)W^{(m)} whose existence is guaranteed by Theorem 2.2. Then, δ=δ(m)\delta=\delta^{(m)} and for any s∈(−δ,δ)s\in(-\delta,\delta),

κ⁡(s)\displaystyle\kappa(s) =κ(m)​(s),\displaystyle=\kappa^{(m)}(s),
pj​(s)\displaystyle p_{j}(s) =0​∀j​ such that ​m∤j,\displaystyle=0\ \forall\ j\ \text{ such that }m\nmid j,
pℓ​m​(s)\displaystyle p_{\ell m}(s) =pℓ(m)​(s),ℓ∈ℕ.\displaystyle=p^{(m)}_{\ell}(s),\ \ell\in\mathbb{N}.

The above relations connect the associated bifurcating branches of stationary solutions with potentials WW and W(m)W^{(m)} in terms of their Fourier coefficients. In particular, if aℓ≠ama_{\ell}\neq a_{m} for all ℓ≠m\ell\neq m, this gives the unique non-trivial branch of solutions at bifurcation point 2/am2/a_{m}.

(b) Assume that, for some m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N}, am>0a_{m}>0. Let S:={ℓ∈ℕ:aℓ=am}S:=\{\ell\in\mathbb{N}:a_{\ell}=a_{m}\}. Further, assume ∑j=1∞j2​aj2<∞\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}j^{2}a_{j}^{2}<\infty (that is, W∈Hs1​(𝕊1)W\in H^{1}_{s}(\mathbb{S}^{1})) and

gcd⁡(S)=g>1.\operatorname{gcd}(S)=g>1.

Then, for any non-trivial branch of solutions (p¯​(s),κ⁡(s)):(−δ,δ)→ℓw2×ℝ+(\underline{p}(s),\kappa(s)):(-\delta,\delta)\rightarrow\ell^{2}_{w}\times\mathbb{R}_{+} around the bifurcation point 2/am2/a_{m}, we must necessarily have δ′∈(0,δ]\delta^{\prime}\in(0,\delta] such that

In other words, the solution is gg-periodic.

Remark 2.2.

The assumption supℓ≥1ℓ​|aℓ|<∞\sup_{\ell\geq 1}\ell|a_{\ell}|<\infty ensures that the Fourier coefficients decay at least as O⁡(1/ℓ)O(1/\ell), implying that

W∈Hsα​(𝕊1):={f⁡(θ)=∑ℓ=1∞fℓ​cos⁡ℓ​θ:∑ℓ=1∞(1+ℓ2)α​fℓ2<∞}W\in H_{s}^{\alpha}(\mathbb{S}^{1}):=\{f(\theta)=\sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty}f_{\ell}\cos\ell\theta:\sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty}(1+\ell^{2})^{\alpha}f_{\ell}^{2}<\infty\}

for every α<12\alpha<\tfrac{1}{2}, but it does not require continuity or boundedness of WW. For example, consider the potential

W⁡(θ)=∑ℓ=1∞cos⁡(ℓ​θ)ℓ=−log⁡(2​sin⁡(θ/2)),θ∈[0,2​π),W(\theta)=\sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty}\frac{\cos(\ell\theta)}{\ell}=-\log\!\big(2\sin(\theta/2)\big),\ \theta\in[0,2\pi),

which we revisit in Section 3 in more detail. It satisfies supℓℓ​|aℓ|<∞\sup_{\ell}\ell|a_{\ell}|<\infty but diverges logarithmically at θ=0\theta=0. In particular, this assumption is strictly weaker than the Zygmund class condition (Zygmund, 2002, Chapter V), which additionally requires uniform control on the discrete derivative aℓ+1−aℓa_{\ell+1}-a_{\ell}.

Remark 2.3.

(a) Suppose a1>a2>⋯>0a_{1}>a_{2}>\dots>0. By Theorem 2.3(a), as the interaction intensity κ\kappa grows (equivalently, if the noise becomes smaller), the periodicity of the non-trivial stationary solutions at subsequent bifurcation points increases. This indicates a form of metastability where the modes of the density which are far enough apart do not strongly interact with each other and thereby persist.

(b) The hypotheses of Theorem 2.3(b) allow for the null-space of the derivative map Dp¯​F​(0¯,2am)D_{\underline{p}}F(\underline{0},\frac{2}{a_{m}}) to have (finite) dimension greater than one, leading to possibly multiple bifurcating non-trivial solutions around κ=2am\kappa=\frac{2}{a_{m}}. Theorem 2.3(b) says that, provided g>1g>1, any such solution is gg-periodic. Theorem 2.3(a) exhibits the existence of an mm-periodic solution.

2.4. Higher order bifurcations

The next result investigates bifurcations at points corresponding to multiple identical Fourier modes of WW, which results in bifurcating stationary solutions with possibly multiple dominant Fourier modes. Even when multiple Fourier modes of WW are not equal but sufficiently close to each other, this result can be used to provide an informal explanation for how this recipe creates ‘approximate’ stationary solutions as candidates for metastable states; see Remark 2.5.

Remark 2.4.

In the setup of Theorem 2.4(a), we make the following observations.

(i) For ℓi∈Λ\ell_{i}\in\Lambda such that Bℓi​ℓi≠0B_{\ell_{i}\ell_{i}}\neq 0, we can take B~\tilde{B} to be the corresponding 1×11\times 1 submatrix and obtain non-trivial unimodal bifurcations (locally ℓi\ell_{i} gives the only dominant mode in the Fourier expansion of pp) for such ℓi\ell_{i}, around κ=2/a\kappa=2/a, as given by Theorem 2.2.

(ii) If Bℓir​ℓirB_{\ell_{i_{r}}\ell_{i_{r}}} are non-zero and of the same sign for some subcollection of indices {i1,…,im}⊂{1,…,k}\{i_{1},\dots,i_{m}\}\subset\{1,\dots,k\} and the off-diagonal terms Bℓir​ℓit,r≠tB_{\ell_{i_{r}}\ell_{i_{t}}},r\neq t are sufficiently small compared to the diagonal terms, Theorem 2.4(a) furnishes a mixed branch of non-trivial solutions where {ℓi1,…,ℓim}\{\ell_{i_{1}},\dots,\ell_{i_{m}}\} all correspond to (local) dominant modes.

(iii) Suppose ℓ,m∈Λ\ell,m\in\Lambda such that Bℓ​ℓ>0,Bm​m>0,Bℓ​m<0,Bm​ℓ<0B_{\ell\ell}>0,B_{mm}>0,B_{\ell m}<0,B_{m\ell}<0 and Bℓ​ℓ​Bm​m−Bℓ​m​Bm​ℓ<0B_{\ell\ell}B_{mm}-B_{\ell m}B_{m\ell}<0. Then, the 2×22\times 2 submatrix B~\tilde{B} constructed from ℓ,m\ell,m satisfies B~−1​𝟏<0\tilde{B}^{-1}\mathbf{1}<0 coordinate-wise. This exhibits instances where there are multiple Fourier modes that all correspond to supercritical (subcritical) unimodal bifurcations but jointly produce a mixed subcritical (supercritical) bifurcation around 2/a2/a.

The resonance condition treated in Theorem 2.4(b) generically produces the only situation with a transcritical bifurcation. More precisely, for the quadratic contribution to survive in the ‘reduced’ Lyapunov-Schmidt system (see Section 4.1 and Lemma 4.4), which produces a transcritical bifurcation, we must necessarily have resonance, namely, l,m∈ℕl,m\in\mathbb{N}, with m<lm<l and l≠2​ml\neq 2m, such that al=am=al+ma_{l}=a_{m}=a_{l+m}. A relaxation of this resonance condition is given as a sufficient condition for a discontinuous phase transition in Carrillo et al. (2020, Section 5.1). In Section 2.6, we show that a branch of non-trivial solutions with κ\kappa values less than 2/a2/a is sufficient to cause such phenomena. Resonance is thus ‘not specially related’ to discontinuous phase transitions, however, resonance is indeed the special structure behind transcritical bifurcations.

Remark 2.5 (Metastability and higher order bifurcations).

Although Theorem 2.4 gives multi-mode bifurcating solutions only when multiple Fourier coefficients of WW agree, at an intuitive level, it also gives useful information when {aℓ:ℓ∈Λ}\{a_{\ell}:\ell\in\Lambda\} are sufficiently close to each other for some finite set Λ\Lambda. If Λ\Lambda satisfies the hypotheses of Theorem 2.4(a), then for any Λ~⊆Λ\tilde{\Lambda}\subseteq\Lambda, one can compute the associated matrix B~\tilde{B} and evaluate B~−1​𝟏\tilde{B}^{-1}\mathbf{1}, provided B~\tilde{B} is invertible; if the entries of B~−1​𝟏\tilde{B}^{-1}\mathbf{1} are nonzero and have the same sign, ‘approximate’ stationary distributions can be computed using the explicit multi-mode pitchfork bifurcating solutions given in Theorem 2.4(a). This approximate stationarity implies that the solution to the McKean-Vlasov equation (1.1) started from such a bifurcating solution remains relatively unchanged over long periods of time, which can be viewed as a form of metastability. A similar analysis can be conducted in the setting of Theorem 2.4(b). Thus, Theorem 2.4 provides a mechanism for obtaining a rich collection of such metastable shapes in the presence of clustering of the Fourier coefficients of WW. See also Corollary 2.1 for a connection between such clustering and discontinuous phase transitions.

2.6. Bifurcations and discontinuous phase transition

With the advent of Optimal Transport, the analysis of the McKean-Vlasov equation has benefited significantly from the viewpoint of (1.1) as a ‘gradient flow’ for the free energy functional (see Chayes and Panferov (2010); Carrillo et al. (2020)). Let 𝒫a​c+​(𝕊1)\mathcal{P}_{ac}^{+}(\mathbb{S}^{1}) denote the space of absolutely continuous probability measures with a strictly positive density. Then, the free energy functional is a map ℱ:𝒫a​c+​(𝕊1)×ℝ+→ℝ\mathcal{F}:\mathcal{P}_{ac}^{+}(\mathbb{S}^{1})\times\mathbb{R}_{+}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} given by

ℱ⁡(ρ,κ):=12​π​∫02​πρ⁡(θ)​log⁡ρ⁡(θ)​𝑑θ−κ8​π2​∫02​π∫02​πW⁡(θ−ϕ)​ρ​(θ)​ρ​(ϕ)​𝑑θ​𝑑ϕ.\displaystyle\mathcal{F}(\rho,\kappa):=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\rho(\theta)\log\rho(\theta)\mathrm{d}\theta-\frac{\kappa}{8\pi^{2}}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}W(\theta-\phi)\rho(\theta)\rho(\phi)\mathrm{d}\theta\mathrm{d}\phi.

Owing to this gradient flow structure, stationary solutions of (1.1), that is, solutions of (1.3), correspond to the critical points of the free energy functional ℱ⁡(⋅,κ)\mathcal{F}(\cdot,\kappa); see Carrillo et al. (2020, Proposition 2.4). Their stability is determined by the local geometry of the energy landscape around these critical points.

The following is obtained from a slight rearrangement of the definitions and propositions in Chayes and Panferov (2010); Carrillo et al. (2020).

Definition 2.2 (Transition point and continuity of phase transition).

A point κc>0\kappa_{c}>0 is said to be a transition point for the McKean-Vlasov equation if (i) for κ<κc\kappa<\kappa_{c}, the uniform distribution p0p_{0} is the unique global minimizer of ℱ⁡(⋅,κ)\mathcal{F}(\cdot,\kappa), (ii) at κ=κc\kappa=\kappa_{c}, p0p_{0} is a global minimizer of ℱ⁡(⋅,κ)\mathcal{F}(\cdot,\kappa), and (iii) for κ>κc\kappa>\kappa_{c}, there exists some ρκ∈𝒫a​c+​(𝕊1)\rho_{\kappa}\in\mathcal{P}_{ac}^{+}(\mathbb{S}^{1}) with ρκ≠p0\rho_{\kappa}\neq p_{0} such that ρκ\rho_{\kappa} is a global minimizer of ℱ⁡(⋅,κ)\mathcal{F}(\cdot,\kappa).

If (i) p0p_{0} is the unique minimizer at κ=κc\kappa=\kappa_{c}, and (ii) for any family of minimizers {ρκ:κ>κc}\{\rho_{\kappa}:\kappa>\kappa_{c}\} we have limκ↓κc‖ρκ−p0‖H1=0\lim_{\kappa\downarrow\kappa_{c}}\|\rho_{\kappa}-p_{0}\|_{H^{1}}=0, where ∥⋅∥H1\|\cdot\|_{H^{1}} is as defined in Section 1.4, κc\kappa_{c} is said to be a continuous transition point. If at least one of these conditions is violated, κc\kappa_{c} is said to be a discontinuous transition point.

The following theorem connects subcritical bifurcations with discontinuous phase transitions.

Theorem 2.6.

Let a:=maxℓ≥1⁡aℓ>0a:=\max_{\ell\geq 1}a_{\ell}>0 and let Λ:={ℓ∈ℕ:aℓ=a}\Lambda:=\{\ell\in\mathbb{N}:a_{\ell}=a\}. Suppose that there exist a nonempty subset Λ′⊆Λ\Lambda^{\prime}\subseteq\Lambda, δ>0\delta>0 and a nontrivial C1C^{1} branch of bifurcating solutions locally around κ∗:=2/a\kappa^{*}:=2/a of the form

p¯​(s)=s​∑i∈Λ′yi​ei+O⁡(s2),p¯′​(s)=∑i∈Λ′yi​ei+O⁡(s),κ⁡(s)∈(0,κ∗)​ for all ​s∈[0,δ),\underline{p}(s)=s\sum_{i\in\Lambda^{\prime}}y_{i}e_{i}+O(s^{2}),\quad\underline{p}^{\prime}(s)=\sum_{i\in\Lambda^{\prime}}y_{i}e_{i}+O(s),\quad\kappa(s)\in(0,\kappa^{*})\text{ for all }s\in[0,\delta),

where yi≠0y_{i}\neq 0 for all i∈Λ′i\in\Lambda^{\prime}. Then κc<κ∗\kappa_{c}<\kappa^{*} and κc\kappa_{c} is a discontinuous phase transition point.

Moreover, there exists ϵ>0\epsilon>0 such that for any potential W~​(θ)=∑ℓ=1∞a~ℓ​cos⁡ℓ​θ\tilde{W}(\theta)=\sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty}\tilde{a}_{\ell}\cos\ell\theta, with ∑ℓ=1∞|aℓ−a~ℓ|<ϵ\sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty}|a_{\ell}-\tilde{a}_{\ell}|<\epsilon, a~:=maxℓ≥1⁡a~ℓ>0\tilde{a}:=\max_{\ell\geq 1}\tilde{a}_{\ell}>0 and the free energy for the associated McKean-Vlasov equation has a discontinuous transition point κ~c<2/a~\tilde{\kappa}_{c}<2/\tilde{a}.

Fig. 4 visually depicts the situation described in Theorem 2.7 in the case of a bifurcation with κ<κ∗\kappa<\kappa^{*} and a single dominant Fourier mode, with modal amplitude plotted along the horizontal axis and κ\kappa along the vertical axis. The ‘local minimum’ corresponds to the transition point κc\kappa_{c} where the global free energy minimizing branch discontinuously transitions from the vertical axis (uniform distribution) to a non-trivial stationary distribution. At κ=κc\kappa=\kappa_{c}, there is ‘coexistence’ in the sense that there are two minimizing solutions with the same free energy but different values of the interaction energy; see Theorem 3.3 for more details.

The following corollary follows immediately from Theorem 2.2, Theorem 2.4 and Theorem 2.6, and identifies conditions for bifurcations with a κ<κ∗\kappa<\kappa^{*} branch, and hence discontinuous phase transitions, to hold.

Corollary 2.1.

Suppose WW satisfies a:=maxℓ≥1⁡aℓ>0a:=\max_{\ell\geq 1}a_{\ell}>0 and one of the following:

  • (i)

    a1>0a_{1}>0, aℓ<a1a_{\ell}<a_{1} for all ℓ≥2\ell\geq 2 and a1/2<a2<a1a_{1}/2<a_{2}<a_{1};

  • (ii)

    The hypotheses of Theorem 2.4(a) with sgn⁡(B~−1​𝟏)<0\operatorname{sgn}\left(\tilde{B}^{-1}\mathbf{1}\right)<0;

  • (iii)

    The hypotheses of Theorem 2.4(b).

Then the associated McKean-Vlasov equation has a discontinuous transition point κ~c<2/a~\tilde{\kappa}_{c}<2/\tilde{a}. The same assertion holds for any potential W~​(θ)=∑ℓ=1∞a~ℓ​cos⁡ℓ​θ\tilde{W}(\theta)=\sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty}\tilde{a}_{\ell}\cos\ell\theta with ∑ℓ=1∞|aℓ−a~ℓ|<ϵ\sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty}|a_{\ell}-\tilde{a}_{\ell}|<\epsilon for sufficiently small ϵ>0\epsilon>0.

Remark 2.7.

Corollary 2.1(iii) can be seen as the analogue of Carrillo et al. (2020, Theorem 5.11). The above theorem and corollary show that a three-mode resonance is just one way in which a discontinuous transition point occurs. The more general cause seems to be a bifurcating branch with κ\kappa values less than 2/a2/a.

2.7. Phase transition for the Noisy Transformer

Recall the Noisy Transformer model described in (1.5). The following result characterizes the continuity of phase transition for the Noisy Transformer model. Before stating the result, we note that the function

R⁡(β):=I2​(β)I1​(β)​ is strictly increasing for ​β>0.R(\beta):=\frac{I_{2}(\beta)}{I_{1}(\beta)}\ \text{ is strictly increasing for }\ \beta>0.
Theorem 2.7 (Phase Transition of Transformer Model).

There exists 0<β−<β+0<\beta_{-}<\beta_{+} such that κ∗​(β)=β/I1​(β)\kappa^{*}(\beta)=\beta/I_{1}(\beta) is a continuous phase transition point for β≤β−\beta\leq\beta_{-} and there exists a discontinuous phase transition point κc​(β)<κ∗​(β)\kappa_{c}(\beta)<\kappa^{*}(\beta) for β>β+\beta>\beta_{+}. Further,

β+≤R−1​(1/2)≈2.447,\beta_{+}\leq R^{-1}(1/2)\approx 2.447,

where the first bifurcation point κ∗​(β)\kappa^{*}(\beta) changes from being supercritical to subcritical as β\beta crosses R−1​(1/2)R^{-1}(1/2).

3. Towards global properties

In general, going beyond local properties for infinite-dimensional non-linear systems like ours is a formidable task, and little can be said in general. In this section, we record some global properties. We hope to address this in greater detail in a subsequent article.

3.1. A ‘singular’ example: log-sine potential and Poisson kernel

The next theorem gives an example of a ‘singular’ potential in the critical bifurcation regime which leads to an explicitly computable global picture with infinitely many bifurcation points.

Theorem 3.1.

Let the interaction potential be given by

WP​o​i​(θ):=−log⁡(2​sin⁡(θ/2))=∑ℓ=1∞1ℓ​cos⁡ℓ​θ,θ∈[0,2​π).\displaystyle W_{Poi}(\theta):=-\log\left(2\sin(\theta/2)\right)=\sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\ell}\cos\ell\theta,\quad\theta\in[0,2\pi).

Then the bifurcation points of (1.3) are precisely κ∈{2​ℓ:ℓ∈ℕ}\kappa\in\{2\ell:\ell\in\mathbb{N}\}. The associated bifurcating non-trivial solutions at κ∗:=2​ℓ∗\kappa^{*}:=2\ell^{*} correspond to the Poisson kernel with wave number ℓ∗\ell^{*} given by

(3.1) Pr,ℓ∗​(θ):=1−r21−2​r​cos⁡(ℓ∗​θ)+r2,θ∈[0,2​π),r∈(−1,1).\displaystyle P_{r,\ell^{*}}(\theta):=\frac{1-r^{2}}{1-2r\cos(\ell^{*}\theta)+r^{2}},\quad\theta\in[0,2\pi),\,r\in(-1,1).

In particular, as r↑1r\uparrow 1, the associated measure μr,ℓ∗​(d​θ):=Pr,ℓ∗​(θ)​d​θ\mu_{r,\ell^{*}}(\mathrm{d}\theta):=P_{r,\ell^{*}}(\theta)\mathrm{d}\theta weakly converges to the sum of Dirac masses 1ℓ∗​∑j=0ℓ∗−1δ2​j​π/ℓ∗\frac{1}{\ell^{*}}\sum_{j=0}^{\ell^{*}-1}\delta_{2j\pi/\ell^{*}} and, as r↓−1r\downarrow-1, μr,ℓ∗​(d​θ)\mu_{r,\ell^{*}}(\mathrm{d}\theta) weakly converges to 1ℓ∗​∑j=0ℓ∗−1δ(π+2​j​π)/ℓ∗\frac{1}{\ell^{*}}\sum_{j=0}^{\ell^{*}-1}\delta_{(\pi+2j\pi)/\ell^{*}}. Moreover, there are no more bifurcation points around any stationary solution.

The Poisson kernel Pr,ℓ​(θ)P_{r,\ell}(\theta) in Eq. 3.1 is a classical object in harmonic analysis, representing the density of the harmonic measure on the unit circle corresponding to the interior point r​ei​0re^{i0} of the unit disk (Rudin, 1987, Section 11.5). Equivalently, it describes how harmonic functions in the disk can be reconstructed from their boundary data via the Poisson integral. In the present context, the appearance of Pr,ℓP_{r,\ell} as a stationary solution of the nonlinear mean-field equation reveals an intriguing connection between collective stochastic dynamics and harmonic analytic structures. Indeed, for the logarithmic sine potential WP​o​iW_{Poi}, the stationary McKean-Vlasov equation reduces to a nonlinear self-consistency relation for the Fourier modes of the Poisson kernel. Each bifurcation point κ=2​ℓ\kappa=2\ell thus marks the onset of a new harmonic mode cos⁡(ℓ​θ)\cos(\ell\theta), and the corresponding branch of stationary measures μr,ℓ\mu_{r,\ell} can be viewed as a nonlinear deformation of the harmonic extension problem on the unit disk.

From the dynamical viewpoint, the limiting regimes r↑1r\uparrow 1 and r↓−1r\downarrow-1 of μr,ℓ\mu_{r,\ell} correspond to extreme “synchronization” phases of the interacting system, where the probability mass concentrates on a finite number of evenly spaced points on the circle. The limiting Dirac masses capture perfect phase alignment (for r↑1r\uparrow 1) and perfect anti-alignment (for r↓−1r\downarrow-1), respectively; see Fig. 5. Hence, the family {μr,ℓ}r∈(−1,1)\{\mu_{r,\ell}\}_{r\in(-1,1)} provides a complete global picture interpolating between the uniform (disordered) state and fully clustered (ordered) configurations. In this sense, the Poisson kernel serves as a canonical bridge between potential theory and the nonlinear geometry of stationary states in McKean-Vlasov dynamics, demonstrating how singular interactions can lead to an infinite cascade of analytically tractable bifurcations.

3.2. A global ‘Kuramoto’ branch

The following result is a simple application of Theorem 2.1 to potentials with finitely many non-zero Fourier coefficients. Stability properties of the associated stationary solutions has been studied recently, both analytically and numerically, by Bertoli et al. (2024). Furthermore, Lucia and Vukadinovic (2010) and Vukadinovic (2023) study the special cases of the Onsager model with a finite mode interaction potential and the Hodgkin-Huxley oscillators, respectively.

Theorem 3.2.

Suppose W⁡(θ)=∑ℓ=1Laℓ​cos⁡ℓ​θ,θ∈[0,2​π)W(\theta)=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}a_{\ell}\cos\ell\theta,\ \theta\in[0,2\pi), where a1>a2>⋯>aℓ>0a_{1}>a_{2}>\dots>a_{\ell}>0. Then, for κ>2/aℓ\kappa>2/a_{\ell}, there exists a global ‘Kuramoto’-type branch of non-trivial solutions given by

πκ​(θ):=LI0​(κ​aℓ​rκ)​exp⁡(κ​aℓ​rκ​cos⁡ℓ​θ),θ∈[0,2​π),\pi_{\kappa}(\theta):=\frac{L}{I_{0}(\kappa a_{\ell}r_{\kappa})}\exp\left(\kappa a_{\ell}r_{\kappa}\cos\ell\theta\right),\quad\theta\in[0,2\pi),

where rκr_{\kappa} is the unique positive solution to

rκ=I1​(κ​aℓ​rκ)I0​(κ​aℓ​rκ).r_{\kappa}=\frac{I_{1}(\kappa a_{\ell}r_{\kappa})}{I_{0}(\kappa a_{\ell}r_{\kappa})}.

Theorem 3.2 thus provides an explicit analytic characterization of the global ‘Kuramoto’-type branch for interaction potentials with finitely many Fourier modes, extending the classical single-mode theory to any dominant harmonic component.

3.3. Global free energy minimizing solutions

The next result collects some observations about the ‘globally free energy minimizing’ solutions of the McKean-Vlasov equation. The proof techniques are quite general and, with natural modifications, the results apply to McKean-Vlasov equations on any compact smooth manifold (e.g. the torus or sphere). Some results in this direction were already obtained in Chayes and Panferov (2010). These observations paint a global picture of the geometry of such solutions. Define for κ>0\kappa>0,

m⁡(κ)\displaystyle m(\kappa) :=infρ∈𝒫a​c+​(𝕊1)ℱ⁡(ρ,κ),\displaystyle:=\inf_{\rho\in\mathcal{P}^{+}_{ac}(\mathbb{S}^{1})}\mathcal{F}(\rho,\kappa),
M⁡(κ)\displaystyle M(\kappa) :={ρ∈𝒫a​c+​(𝕊1):ℱ⁡(ρ,κ)=m⁡(κ)}.\displaystyle:=\{\rho\in\mathcal{P}^{+}_{ac}(\mathbb{S}^{1}):\mathcal{F}(\rho,\kappa)=m(\kappa)\}.

Writing ∫\int for 12​π∫02​π\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}, we define the interaction energy of ρ∈𝒫a​c+​(𝕊1)\rho\in\mathcal{P}^{+}_{ac}(\mathbb{S}^{1}) as

ℰ⁡(ρ,ρ):=∬W⁡(θ−ϕ)​ρ​(θ)​ρ​(ϕ)​𝑑θ​𝑑ϕ.\mathcal{E}(\rho,\rho):=\iint W(\theta-\phi)\rho(\theta)\rho(\phi)\mathrm{d}\theta\mathrm{d}\phi.
Theorem 3.3.

Assume WW is continuous and ‖W‖∞<∞\|W\|_{\infty}<\infty. The minimum energy map κ↦m⁡(κ)\kappa\mapsto m(\kappa) and the set map of minimizers κ↦M⁡(κ)\kappa\mapsto M(\kappa) satisfy the following.

(i) For every κ>0\kappa>0, M⁡(κ)M(\kappa) is non-empty and compact in L1​(𝕊1)L^{1}(\mathbb{S}^{1}). Moreover, if κn→κ∘\kappa_{n}\to\kappa^{\circ} and ρκn∈M⁡(κn)\rho_{\kappa_{n}}\in M(\kappa_{n}), then there exists a subsequence {nj}\{n_{j}\} such that ρnj→ρ∘∈M⁡(κ∘)\rho_{n_{j}}\to\rho^{\circ}\in M(\kappa^{\circ}) in L1​(𝕊1)L^{1}(\mathbb{S}^{1}) (sequential compactness in ℝ+×L1​(𝕊1)\mathbb{R}_{+}\times L^{1}(\mathbb{S}^{1})).

(ii) The map κ↦m⁡(κ)\kappa\mapsto m(\kappa) is concave and globally Lipschitz. Its left and right derivatives m−′,m+′m^{\prime}_{-},m^{\prime}_{+} exist for all κ>0\kappa>0. They further satisfy the ‘envelope identities’

m−′(κ)=−12infρ∈M⁡(κ)ℰ(ρ,ρ),m+′(κ)=−12supρ∈M⁡(κ)ℰ(ρ,ρ).\displaystyle m^{\prime}_{-}(\kappa)=-\frac{1}{2}\inf_{\rho\in M(\kappa)}\mathcal{E}(\rho,\rho),\quad m^{\prime}_{+}(\kappa)=-\frac{1}{2}\sup_{\rho\in M(\kappa)}\mathcal{E}(\rho,\rho).

The maps κ↦infρ∈M⁡(κ)ℰ⁡(ρ,ρ)\kappa\mapsto\inf_{\rho\in M(\kappa)}\mathcal{E}(\rho,\rho) and κ↦supρ∈M⁡(κ)ℰ⁡(ρ,ρ)\kappa\mapsto\sup_{\rho\in M(\kappa)}\mathcal{E}(\rho,\rho) are non-decreasing in κ\kappa.

(iii) There are at most countably many points of non-differentiability (‘kinks’) of κ↦m⁡(κ)\kappa\mapsto m(\kappa). At such a point κ\kappa, M⁡(κ)M(\kappa) has at least two elements (called ‘coexistence’ points) which both minimize the free energy but have different values of the interaction energy.

Remark 3.1.

Suppose maxℓ⁡aℓ>0\max_{\ell}a_{\ell}>0. Combining part (iii) above with Carrillo et al. (2020, Proposition 5.8) we conclude that mm has a kink at some point κc<2/maxℓ⁡aℓ\kappa_{c}<2/\max_{\ell}a_{\ell} if and only if κc\kappa_{c} is a discontinuous transition point. Otherwise, there is a continuous transition at κ=2/maxℓ⁡aℓ\kappa=2/\max_{\ell}a_{\ell} after which the uniform distribution is no longer a minimizer (see Gates and Penrose (1970)) and a globally free energy minimizing branch continuously bifurcates from the trivial branch. Nevertheless, there could be subsequent kinks in the path of κ↦m⁡(κ)\kappa\mapsto m(\kappa) for κ>2/maxℓ⁡aℓ\kappa>2/\max_{\ell}a_{\ell} producing discontinuous transitions with respect to some non-trivial global minimizer(s).

4.1. Lyapunov-Schmidt reduction

The proofs of our results rely on the so-called Lyapunov-Schmidt reduction (Kielhöfer, 2012, Theorem I.2.3) which transforms the problem of characterizing zero sets in infinite-dimensional Banach spaces into essentially a finite-dimensional one by careful applications of the (Banach space version of the) Implicit Function Theorem (Kielhöfer, 2012, Theorem I.1.1). We first cast our problem in this general set-up, where we mainly follow Kielhöfer (2012). First, note that F⁡(0¯,κ)=0F(\underline{0},\kappa)=0 for all κ>0\kappa>0. Moreover, from Lemma 2.1,

(4.1) [Dp¯​F​(0¯,κ)​h¯]ℓ=ℓ⁡(2−κ​aℓ)​hℓ,ℓ∈ℕ.\displaystyle\left[D_{\underline{p}}F(\underline{0},\kappa)\underline{h}\right]_{\ell}=\ell(2-\kappa a_{\ell})h_{\ell},\quad\ell\in\mathbb{N}.

Suppose, for some κ∗∈ℝ+\kappa^{*}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}, there are exactly kk Fourier modes {aℓ1,…,aℓk}\{a_{\ell_{1}},\dots,a_{\ell_{k}}\} such that aℓj=2/κ∗a_{\ell_{j}}=2/\kappa^{*} for 1≤j≤k1\leq j\leq k. Thus, the dimension of the kernel and co-dimension of the range of Dp¯​F​(0¯,κ∗)D_{\underline{p}}F(\underline{0},\kappa^{*}) are both kk. Moreover, as Dp¯​F​(0¯,κ∗)D_{\underline{p}}F(\underline{0},\kappa^{*}) is a diagonal mapping, it is easy to check that its range is closed. Thus, FF is a nonlinear Fredholm operator of index zero (Kielhöfer, 2012, Definition I.2.1). Consequently, there exist closed complements in the Banach spaces ℓw2\ell^{2}_{w} and ℓ2\ell^{2} such that

ℓw2=N⊕X0,ℓ2=R⊕Z0,\displaystyle\ell^{2}_{w}=N\oplus X_{0},\qquad\ell^{2}=R\oplus Z_{0},

where N=kerDp¯F(0¯,κ∗)=span[{eℓ1,…,eℓk}]:={x¯∈ℓw2:xℓ=0∀ℓ≠ℓ1,…,ℓk}N=\operatorname{ker}D_{\underline{p}}F(\underline{0},\kappa^{*})=\operatorname{span}[\{e_{\ell_{1}},\dots,e_{\ell_{k}}\}]:=\{\underline{x}\in\ell_{w}^{2}:x_{\ell}=0\ \forall\ \ell\neq\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{k}\} and R=Ran⁡Dp¯​F​(0¯,κ∗)={x¯∈ℓ2:xℓj=0​ for all ​1≤j≤k}R=\operatorname{Ran}D_{\underline{p}}F(\underline{0},\kappa^{*})=\{\underline{x}\in\ell^{2}:x_{\ell_{j}}=0\text{ for all }1\leq j\leq k\}. Q​F​(u+w,κ)=0​ and ​(I−Q)​F​(u+w,κ)=0,\displaystyle QF(u+w,\kappa)=0\ \text{ and }\ (I-Q)F(u+w,\kappa)=0,

where u=P​xu=Px and w=(I−P)​xw=(I-P)x. Using the invertibility of Dp¯​F​(0¯,κ∗)D_{\underline{p}}F(\underline{0},\kappa^{*}) on RR and the Implicit Function Theorem, we can obtain open sets U~⊂N\tilde{U}\subset N, W~⊂X0\tilde{W}\subset X_{0}, V⊂ℝ+V\subset\mathbb{R}_{+} and a C1C^{1} function Ψ:U~×V→W~\Psi:\tilde{U}\times V\rightarrow\tilde{W} satisfying Ψ⁡(0¯,κ∗)=0\Psi(\underline{0},\kappa^{*})=0 such that

Let the hypotheses in Theorem 2.4(b) hold. For any non-trivial branch of solutions to (4.8) locally around κ=2/a\kappa=2/a, we have the following reduced system of Lyapunov-Schmidt equations:

for sufficiently small ‖χ¯‖w\|\underline{\chi}\|_{w}.

Similarly, the only such quadratic contribution in (4.8) when ℓ=m\ell=m also comes from j=l+mj=l+m. Finally, when ℓ=l+m\ell=l+m, the only contributions now come from the first sum when j=l,mj=l,m.

The remaining terms are O⁡(‖χ¯‖w3)O\left(\|\underline{\chi}\|_{w}^{3}\right) by (4.10). The lemma follows. ∎

and ρn∈M⁡(κ+hn)\rho_{n}\in M(\kappa+h_{n}). Note that

m⁡(κ+hn)−m⁡(κ)≥ℱ⁡(ρn,κ+hn)−ℱ⁡(ρn,κ)=−hn2​ℰ​(ρn,ρn).m(\kappa+h_{n})-m(\kappa)\geq\mathcal{F}(\rho_{n},\kappa+h_{n})-\mathcal{F}(\rho_{n},\kappa)=-\frac{h_{n}}{2}\mathcal{E}(\rho_{n},\rho_{n}).

Moreover, by part (i), there is a subsequence {nj}\{n_{j}\} such that ρnj→ρ∗∈M⁡(κ)\rho_{n_{j}}\rightarrow\rho^{*}\in M(\kappa) in L1​(𝕊1)L^{1}(\mathbb{S}^{1}) (and thus, weakly), and as WW is bounded and continuous, ℰ⁡(ρnj,ρnj)→ℰ⁡(ρ∗,ρ∗).\mathcal{E}(\rho_{n_{j}},\rho_{n_{j}})\to\mathcal{E}(\rho^{*},\rho^{*}). Thus,

(7.4) lim infh↓0m⁡(κ+h)−m⁡(κ)h=limj→∞m⁡(κ+hnj)−m⁡(κ)hnj≥−12ℰ(ρ∗,ρ∗)≥−12supρ∈M⁡(κ)ℰ(ρ,ρ).\displaystyle\liminf_{h\downarrow 0}\frac{m(\kappa+h)-m(\kappa)}{h}=\lim_{j\to\infty}\frac{m(\kappa+h_{n_{j}})-m(\kappa)}{h_{n_{j}}}\geq-\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{E}(\rho^{*},\rho^{*})\geq-\frac{1}{2}\sup_{\rho\in M(\kappa)}\mathcal{E}(\rho,\rho).

From (7.3) and (7.4), we conclude that limh↓0m⁡(κ+h)−m⁡(κ)h\lim_{h\downarrow 0}\frac{m(\kappa+h)-m(\kappa)}{h} exists and

m+′(κ):=limh↓0m⁡(κ+h)−m⁡(κ)h=−12supρ∈M⁡(κ)ℰ(ρ,ρ).m^{\prime}_{+}(\kappa):=\lim_{h\downarrow 0}\frac{m(\kappa+h)-m(\kappa)}{h}=-\frac{1}{2}\sup_{\rho\in M(\kappa)}\mathcal{E}(\rho,\rho).

The left derivative can be handled similarly. The monotonicity properties of supρ∈M⁡(κ)ℰ⁡(ρ,ρ)\sup_{\rho\in M(\kappa)}\mathcal{E}(\rho,\rho) and infρ∈M⁡(κ)ℰ⁡(ρ,ρ)\inf_{\rho\in M(\kappa)}\mathcal{E}(\rho,\rho) follow exactly as in Chayes and Panferov (2010, Proposition 2.4). This completes the proof of (ii).

Finally, to prove (iii), note that by the concavity of mm, for any 0<a<b0<a<b,

m+′​(a)≥m⁡(b)−m⁡(a)b−a≥m−′​(b).m^{\prime}_{+}(a)\geq\frac{m(b)-m(a)}{b-a}\geq m^{\prime}_{-}(b).

Let κ>0\kappa>0 be a continuity point of both m+′m^{\prime}_{+} and m−′m^{\prime}_{-}. Taking a=κ−ha=\kappa-h, b=κ+hb=\kappa+h (for small enough h>0h>0) above and taking a limit as h↓0h\downarrow 0, we obtain

m+′​(κ)≥limh↓0m⁡(κ+h)−m⁡(κ−h)2​h≥m−′​(κ).m^{\prime}_{+}(\kappa)\geq\lim_{h\downarrow 0}\frac{m(\kappa+h)-m(\kappa-h)}{2h}\geq m^{\prime}_{-}(\kappa).

But, from part (ii), m+′​(κ)≤m−′​(κ)m^{\prime}_{+}(\kappa)\leq m^{\prime}_{-}(\kappa). Hence,

m+′​(κ)=limh↓0m⁡(κ+h)−m⁡(κ−h)2​h=m−′​(κ),m^{\prime}_{+}(\kappa)=\lim_{h\downarrow 0}\frac{m(\kappa+h)-m(\kappa-h)}{2h}=m^{\prime}_{-}(\kappa),

which gives the differentiability of mm at κ\kappa. Thus, the points of non-differentiability of mm form a subset of the set of discontinuity points of either m+′m^{\prime}_{+} or m−′m^{\prime}_{-} or both. But this set is at most countable as m+′m^{\prime}_{+} and m−′m^{\prime}_{-} are both monotone, proving (iii). ∎

Appendix A Justification for Section 2.5.1

Here, we provide details about the explicit analytical description of the bifurcating solutions pκ±​(θ)p_{\kappa}^{\pm}(\theta) near the bifurcation point via various approximations. Note that we have the following:

  1. (1)

    Amplitude term s±​(κ)s^{\pm}(\kappa). The leading order in ε=κ​am−2\varepsilon=\kappa a_{m}-2, is given by

    s±​(κ)=±ε​am−a2​mam−2​a2​m+O⁡(|ε|3/2).s^{\pm}(\kappa)=\pm\sqrt{\varepsilon\,\frac{a_{m}-a_{2m}}{a_{m}-2a_{2m}}}+O(|\varepsilon|^{3/2}).

    Substituting aℓ=2​Iℓ​(β)βa_{\ell}=\tfrac{2I_{\ell}(\beta)}{\beta} then yields

    s±​(κ)=±(κ​2​Im​(β)β−2)​Im​(β)−I2​m​(β)Im​(β)−2​I2​m​(β)+O⁡(|κ​am−2|3/2).s^{\pm}(\kappa)=\pm\sqrt{\left(\kappa\frac{2I_{m}(\beta)}{\beta}-2\right)\frac{I_{m}(\beta)-I_{2m}(\beta)}{I_{m}(\beta)-2I_{2m}(\beta)}}+O(|\kappa a_{m}-2|^{3/2}).

    The sign/branch and whether these appear for κ>κm\kappa>\kappa_{m} (supercritical) or κ<κm\kappa<\kappa_{m} (subcritical) is determined by the mm-signature, i.e., the sign of Rm​(β)=(am−2​a2​m)/(am−2​a2​m)R_{m}(\beta)=(a_{m}-2a_{2m})/(a_{m}-2a_{2m}), as described in Theorem 2.5.

  2. (2)

    Recursive coefficients zℓ​m​(κ)z_{\ell m}(\kappa). By definition zm​(κ)=1z_{m}(\kappa)=1. For ℓ=2\ell=2 the recursion (2.10) gives

    z2​m​(κ)=κ​am2​(2−κ​a2​m),z_{2m}(\kappa)=\frac{\kappa a_{m}}{2(2-\kappa a_{2m})},

    and at κ=κm\kappa=\kappa_{m} this simplifies to

    z2​m​(κm)=am2​(am−a2​m)=Im​(β)2​(Im​(β)−I2​m​(β)).z_{2m}(\kappa_{m})=\frac{a_{m}}{2(a_{m}-a_{2m})}=\frac{I_{m}(\beta)}{2\bigl(I_{m}(\beta)-I_{2m}(\beta)\bigr)}.
  3. (3)

    Explicit two-term approximation. Keeping only the dominant ℓ=1\ell=1 and ℓ=2\ell=2 terms in the exponent and using the leading-order amplitudes above, one obtains the approximation

    pκ±​(θ)≈1Z​exp⁡(κ​am​s±​(κ)​cos⁡(m​θ)⏟primary mode+κ​a2​m​z2​m​(κm)​(s±​(κ))2​cos⁡(2​m​θ)⏟second harmonic),p_{\kappa}^{\pm}(\theta)\approx\frac{1}{Z}\exp\Big(\underbrace{\kappa a_{m}s^{\pm}(\kappa)\cos(m\theta)}_{\text{primary mode}}+\underbrace{\kappa a_{2m}\,z_{2m}(\kappa_{m})\,(s^{\pm}(\kappa))^{2}\cos(2m\theta)}_{\text{second harmonic}}\Big),

    where ZZ normalizes the density. The omitted terms (higher harmonics, the remainders rℓ​mr_{\ell m}, and error on replacing z2​m​(κ)z_{2m}(\kappa) by z2​m​(κm)z_{2m}(\kappa_{m})) contribute O⁡(|κ​am−2|3/2)O(|\kappa a_{m}-2|^{3/2}) or smaller corrections in the exponent, so the leading structure is a primary cosine wave of frequency mm with a smaller second-harmonic contribution of frequency 2​m2m whose magnitude is quadratic in the primary amplitude.

Small-β\beta explicit approximation.

For small β>0\beta>0 use the leading small-β\beta approximation

Iℓ​(β)≈(β/2)ℓℓ!(β↓0),aℓ=2​Iℓ​(β)β≈βℓ−12ℓ−1​ℓ!.I_{\ell}(\beta)\approx\frac{(\beta/2)^{\ell}}{\ell!}\quad(\beta\downarrow 0),\qquad a_{\ell}=\frac{2I_{\ell}(\beta)}{\beta}\approx\frac{\beta^{\ell-1}}{2^{\ell-1}\,\ell!}.

Set

κm=2am,Δ≔κam−2(so Δ=am(κ−κm)).\kappa_{m}=\frac{2}{a_{m}},\qquad\Delta\coloneqq\kappa a_{m}-2\quad(\text{so }\Delta=a_{m}(\kappa-\kappa_{m})).

For |Δ|≪1|\Delta|\ll 1 and a2​m≪ama_{2m}\ll a_{m} we may approximate

s±​(κ)=±Δ+O⁡(|Δ|3/2),z2​m​(κm)=am2​(am−a2​m)=12+O⁡(a2​mam).s^{\pm}(\kappa)=\pm\sqrt{\Delta}+O(|\Delta|^{3/2}),\qquad z_{2m}(\kappa_{m})=\frac{a_{m}}{2(a_{m}-a_{2m})}=\frac{1}{2}+O\!\Big(\frac{a_{2m}}{a_{m}}\Big).

Using s±​(κ)≈±Δs^{\pm}(\kappa)\approx\pm\sqrt{\Delta} and κ​am≈2\kappa a_{m}\approx 2 (to leading order) we have

pκ±​(θ)≈1Z​exp⁡(±2​Δ​cos⁡(m​θ)+12​κ​a2​m​Δ​cos⁡(2​m​θ)).p_{\kappa}^{\pm}(\theta)\approx\frac{1}{Z}\exp\Big(\pm 2\sqrt{\Delta}\,\cos(m\theta)+\tfrac{1}{2}\,\kappa a_{2m}\,\Delta\,\cos(2m\theta)\Big).

am≈βm−12m−1​m!,a2​m≈β2​m−12 2​m−1​(2​m)!,a_{m}\approx\frac{\beta^{m-1}}{2^{\,m-1}m!},\qquad a_{2m}\approx\frac{\beta^{2m-1}}{2^{\,2m-1}(2m)!},

gives the most explicit small-β\beta form

pκ±​(θ)≈1Z​exp⁡(±2​βm−12m−1​m!​(κ−κm)​cos⁡(m​θ)+O⁡(β2​m−1​(κ−κm))).p_{\kappa}^{\pm}(\theta)\approx\frac{1}{Z}\exp\Bigg(\pm 2\sqrt{\frac{\beta^{m-1}}{2^{\,m-1}m!}\,(\kappa-\kappa_{m})}\cos(m\theta)+O\!\big(\beta^{2m-1}(\kappa-\kappa_{m})\big)\Bigg).

Here the O⁡(⋅)O(\cdot) term denotes the second-harmonic amplitude (and higher-harmonic contributions) which are parametrically small in β\beta.

Large-β\beta explicit approximation.

Note that for fixed mm and β→∞\beta\to\infty, we have the estimate from Eq. 2.6 for ama_{m}. Hence, we have

am−a2​m=C⁡(β)​[3​m22​β+O⁡(1β2)],am−2​a2​m=C⁡(β)​[−1+28​m2−18​β+O⁡(1β2)],whereC⁡(β)=2​eββ3/2​2​π.\begin{aligned} a_{m}-a_{2m}&=C(\beta)\!\left[\frac{3m^{2}}{2\beta}+O\!\left(\frac{1}{\beta^{2}}\right)\right],\\[6.0pt] a_{m}-2a_{2m}&=C(\beta)\!\left[-1+\frac{28m^{2}-1}{8\beta}+O\!\left(\frac{1}{\beta^{2}}\right)\right],\end{aligned}\qquad\text{where}\quad C(\beta)=\frac{2e^{\beta}}{\beta^{3/2}\sqrt{2\pi}}.

So am−a2​m>0a_{m}-a_{2m}>0 while am−2​a2​m<0a_{m}-2a_{2m}<0 for large β\beta. Therefore, the ratio

am−2​a2​mam−a2​m<0,\frac{a_{m}-2a_{2m}}{a_{m}-a_{2m}}<0,

and the bifurcation is subcritical, i.e., non-trivial solutions appear for κ<κm\kappa<\kappa_{m}.

Let δ≔2−κ​am\delta\coloneqq 2-\kappa a_{m} (small and positive on the subcritical branch). Substituting the above asymptotics in the general amplitude formula, gives the explicit large-β\beta scaling

s±​(κ)=±3​m22​β​δ+O⁡(δ​β−1,δ3/2).s^{\pm}(\kappa)=\pm\sqrt{\frac{3m^{2}}{2\beta}\,\delta}+O\!\big(\delta\beta^{-1},\delta^{3/2}\big).

Similarly, for the recursive coefficient at the bifurcation point,

z2​m​(κm)=am2​(am−a2​m)∼β3​m2​(1+O⁡(β−1)).z_{2m}(\kappa_{m})=\frac{a_{m}}{2(a_{m}-a_{2m})}\sim\frac{\beta}{3m^{2}}\big(1+O(\beta^{-1})\big).

Keeping the dominant ℓ=m\ell=m (primary) and ℓ=2​m\ell=2m (second-harmonic) terms in the exponent and using κ​am=2−δ\kappa a_{m}=2-\delta, we obtain the explicit two-term approximation for the density near the bifurcation as

pκ±​(θ)≈1Z​exp⁡(±2​3​m22​β​δ​cos⁡(m​θ)+δ​cos⁡(2​m​θ))+(smaller order corrections).p_{\kappa}^{\pm}(\theta)\approx\frac{1}{Z}\exp\Bigg(\pm 2\sqrt{\frac{3m^{2}}{2\beta}\,\delta}\,\cos(m\theta)+\delta\,\cos(2m\theta)\Bigg)+\text{(smaller order corrections)}.

Here the omitted terms are O⁡(δ3/2)O(\delta^{3/2}) or smaller in the exponent and correspond to higher harmonics and remainder terms.
